full_judgment:
This First Miscellaneous Appeal at the instance of the petitioner-appellant is directed against the judgment and order dated 20th January, 1985 passed by Mrs. NA Sultana, Subordinate Judge, Tangail in Miscellaneous Case No. 107 of 1977 setting aside the award dated 3rd September, 1983. 

 2. Short facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The petitioner as appellant since dead and substituted by his heirs, the present appellants and the opposite parties-respondents 1-4 formed a partnership firm in the name of Rupali Traders and executed a deed of partnership on 1-1-76. The said partnership firm commenced its business from 1-1-76 for manufacturing bricks and to supply the same to different buyers; that the partnership business continued quite well but in spite of the request of the said petitioner late Khitish Chandra Debnath the other partners were not rendering any account and giving any profit money to the said petitioner. All the attempts of the petitioner for getting accounts of the bills failed. He therefore, in terms of Clause 17 of the partnership deed issued notice upon the opposite parties on 2-6-77 asking for nomination of arbitrators with a view to resolve the dispute by arbitration amongst the partners of the firm and to settle the accounts of their business. But in spite of the notice from the petitioner, the opposite parties did not respond to the said notice and the petitioner therefore, was constrained to file an application before the court of the Subordinate and District delegate Tangail under section 8 of the Arbitration Act for appointment of arbitrators to take account and verify the stock of the partnership business and to give an award accordingly. The opposite parties on receipt of the notice then appeared in court and filed their written objection against the said application for appointment of arbitrators. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both the sides was pleased to reject the prayer of the petitioner for appointment of arbitrators. Thereafter, the petitioner moved this court and got an order in his favour for appointment of arbitrators. This court directed the learned Subordinate Judge to appoint arbitrators in terms of clause 17 of the partnership deed as per decision in Civil Revision Case No. 1624/78. The opposite-parties being aggrieved by the same preferred a leave petition for appeal before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh being No. 330/82. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division after hearing the leave petition were pleased to uphold the judgment and order of the High Court Division and dismissed the same with the following observation: 

 "17. That all other matters for which no provision have been made in this deed shall be decided by all the partners mutually and will be governed by the Partnership Act. In the case of any difference of opinion amongst the partners it shall be decided by the partners mutually, but if the partners fail, the same shall be referred to an Arbitration Board and in that case each of the partners shall appoint an arbitrator and all the partners shall appoint another arbitrator and the decision of that Arbitration Board consisting of 6(six) members shall be final and binding upon the partners." 

 Accordingly, the Arbitration Board consisting of 6 members was formed by this court on 3-3-83 to take account and verify the stock of the disputed firm and to find out what amount was due to the petitioner and to be paid by the opposite parties and to give an award to that effect. The Arbitration Board accordingly went into action and ultimately submitted an award with the finding that the partnership business in question was still subsisting and that a total amount of Taka 4,27,859.00 was due to the partner petitioner and to be paid by the opposite parties. The petitioner i.e. the appellant, thereafter filed this award in the aforesaid court to make the same a Rule of the court under section 17 of the Arbitration Act and to pass a decree accordingly. The opposite parties-respondents filed 2 sets of written objections against the said award and contended, inter alia, that the Arbitrators misconducted themselves and the award was not made by majority of the Arbitrators and the same was improperly procured and, as such, liable to be set aside. It was further alleged in the objection that on 3-9-83 there was a meeting of the Arbitrators in connection with the arbitration but no decision could be arrived at in that meeting and it was decided that there could be another meeting for the said purpose, but meanwhile the petitioner/appellant most collusively and fraudulently created the impugned award behind the back of the arbitrators and somehow procured the signatures of only 3 of them on the same by fraudulent means. However both the sides adduced evidence in support of their respective cases. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner appellant that the award was a genuine one and it was free from all brassiness and that in the meeting of the arbitrators held on 3-9-83, one of the Arbitrators Kazi Mazharul Islam was not present and the award was made in presence of 5 arbitrators only out of whom the 3 arbitrators signed the award and, as such, the award was legal and given by a majority of the arbitrators, and it was further contended that the said Kazi Mazharul Islam subsequently was present in the meeting of the Board on 3-9-83 to make the impugned award invalid. On behalf of the petitioner, 3 witnesses namely M/s SM Serajul Islam, Md. Jahangir Hossain Khan and Md. Shahjahan Miah, the Arbitrators were examined as PWs. 1, 2 and 3. On behalf of the opposite parties there were 4 DWs. The said Kazi Mazharul Islam, one of the Arbitrators, deposed as DW 2 and stated that in the said meeting of the Board on 3-9-83 he attended but he was a bit late by 15/20 minutes and after attending the meeting he put his signature in the list of the members present in the meeting. He has stated in his deposition that in the meeting no decision was taken by the Arbitrators and no paper was scrutinised and no deposition of the witnesses was recorded. DW 3 Jaharul Hoque Khan, another arbitrator, corroborated the case of the objectors. He also stated that in the said meeting no decision could be arrived at and no papers were scrutinised and no award was written and that there was evidence of one Md. Mahinuddin, the arbitrator who deposed as DW 4 and corroborated the case of the objectors. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record and hearing the parties came to a finding that on 3-9-83 no decision was actually arrived at and no award was written and that all the 6 arbitrators were present but the alleged award was signed by only 3 members of the Board and, as such, it was not an award by the majority of the arbitrators and therefore invalid. Considering all aspects of the case, the impugned award was found not to have been procured legally and properly and according to the observation of their Lordships of the Appellate Division to the effect that the Arbitrators should at first find whether the disputed partnership business was still in existence, before taking up the dispute for arbitration. Of course, on the question of limitation raised by the petitioner in respect of the objections filed by the objectors, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the objections were within time. In the ultimate decision, the learned Subordinate Judge could not accept the award as genuine and legal and accordingly set aside the same by his judgment and order dated 20-1-85 fixing 9-2-1985 for taking necessary steps by the parties. Being aggrieved by the same the petitioner Khitish Chandra Debnath since deceased and substituted by his heirs appellant. No. 1(1) to 1(4) preferred this present Miscellaneous Appeal in this court. 

 3. Md. Abdur Rashid, the learned Advocate appeared for the petitioner-appellant and Mr. Gour Gopal Saha the learned Advocate appeared for the opposite parties-respondents. The learned Advocate for the appellant after taking me through the impugned judgment and other relevant papers available on the record has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed illegality in not remitting the award of the arbitrators for re-consideration in exercise of power under section 16 of the Arbitration Act, in view of the fact that the Arbitrators failed to comply with the direction of the Appellate Division and to decide first whether the business of the firm MIs Rupali Traders was continuing or dissolved on 10-11-76 after final accounting and distribution of the assets. He has not found so much of fault with the arbitration proceeding or with the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge, but his grievance is that the direction of their Lordships of the Appellate Division having not been first complied with, it was a fit case for remittance to the Arbitrators for reconsideration under section 16 of the Arbitration Act. In support of his contention he has relied on a decision in the case of Prokash Narayan Moda & ors. vs. Durga Datta Moda and ors, reported in 1970 Supreme Court Cases Vol. 3 page 190 and also on a decision in the case of Narayan Das Hari Varesh vs. Kanpur Nagar Mohapalika reported in AIR 1963 Allahabad 269. 

 4. Mr. Gour Gopal Saha, the learned Advocate for the respondents, on the other hand, submitted that on the face of it, the award was illegal as the same was not made by a majority as required under Clause 17 of the partnership deed regarding arbitration and also on perusal of the impugned judgment it transpires that the arbitrators misconducted themselves from the very beginning and admittedly the direction of the Appellate Division was not complied with and further all the questions involved in the arbitration including taking stocks of the properties of the partnership business and verification thereof were not done and that the decision as to the award allegedly taken in a meeting of the arbitrators on 3-9-83 was also found to be false and thus the alleged award was illegally procured. The learned Advocate for the respondents therefore submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly set aside the award and fixed a date for further steps by the parties, by the impugned judgment and the same suffered from no illegality justifying any interference by this court. 

 5. As regards the submissions of Mr. Rashid, the learned Advocate for the appellant, for remitting the award to the arbitrators for re-consideration under section 16 of the Arbitration Act, it is submitted by the learned Advocate for the respondents that exercise of power under section 16 of the Arbitration Act is not warranted and justified in the facts and circumstances of this case and apart from that exercise of such power under section 16 of the Arbitration Act is discretionary with the court concerned. The learned Subordinate Judge, according to him, has rightly set aside the award on cogent ground of misconduct and non-compliance of the provisions of law and direction of the superior court and fixed another date for taking steps by the parties, instead of sending the same to the arbitrators for re-consideration under section 16 of the Arbitration Act. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the respondents has referred to a decision in the case of M/s AZ Company, Karachi vs. Messers S. Nauta Bukhsh Muhammad Bashir, Karachi, reported in 17 DLR (SC) 404. 

 6. Mr. Saha had raised further point in this appeal as to the necessity for appointment of umpire in case of even number of arbitrators. It is true that there is no specific mention in the deed of agreement even in its Clause 17 which provides for appointment of an Arbitration Board consisting of 6 members, that means a Board of even numbers, but there is no provision for appointment of any umpire to take final decision in case of tie in the matter of arbitration amongst the arbitrators. It has been pointed out to me from section 3 of the Arbitration Act that in case of absence of such provision of any agreements, the provisions for appointment of umpire as set out in the First Schedule of the Arbitration Act should be deemed to be included in the arbitration agreement and, as such, applicable to the reference. 

 Hence, in view of section 3 of the Arbitration Act, Mr. Saha, the learned Advocate for the respondents, submits that for appointment of umpire there is provision in para 2 of the 1st Schedule of the Arbitration Act which is applicable to the instant case. Para 2 of the Ist Schedule is in the following terms: 

 Mr. Saha thus relying on the above provision further submits that there has been material irregularity, rather illegality, in not appointing an umpire in this case, when the board of arbitrators consisted of 6 members only i.e. even numbers. 

 7. I have heard and considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates and examined the relevant provisions of law and the agreement in the instant case. According to my view, para 2 of the 1st Schedule of the Arbitration Act is very much applicable to this case and as the Board of Arbitrators constituted under Clause 17 of the agreement consisted of 6 members, that means of even numbers, they ought to have appointed an umpire within the prescribed time as per the above law, but that having not been done the arbitrators committed illegality in proceeding with the arbitration and. making the disputed award by a so-called majority of the arbitrators. As regards appointment of an umpire in the case of the expiry of the specified time, I think recourse may be taken to the provision for appointment of umpire by the court on the prayer of the parties as per section 8(1)(c) of the Arbitration Act. Referring to the facts of the case and the evidence on record, Mr. Saha submits that it is apparent on the face of the award that the same was illegally procured and the arbitrators misconducted themselves in making the same and the award therefore has been rightly set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge. In support of his contention, he has relied on a decision in the case of Badrilal vs. Lakshya and others, reported in AIR 1936 Nag. 191. He has also relied on a decision in this regard in the case of Hashmat Ali Jamaddar & ors. vs. Asmatal Jamaddar reported in 6 DLR 478. 

 8. Mr. Saha, the learned Advocate for the respondents, however, submits that the impugned judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are perfectly valid and legal and the same do not call for any interference by this court. He, however, concludes his submission by expressing his no objection to any fresh arbitration in the matter by a fresh set of arbitrators in accordance with the provision of the agreement and the relevant laws and his anxiety is that when misconduct has been found by the court in the matter of arbitration by some of the arbitrators, it is wiser and better if the fresh arbitration is held by a new set of arbitrators. The learned Advocate for the appellant Mr. Rashid ultimately also conceded to this. However it is found that there has been a lot of illegalities and irregularities in making the award and, as such, he has no objection if a fresh arbitration is directed with a fresh set of arbitrators in accordance with the agreement and the relevant laws. In consideration of the above submissions of the learned Advocates, the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, I am of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly set aside the award and there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order.
